narrative:

It sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, and this gap strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your family income being in the middle bracket also increased the likelihood of failure, though less dramatically; among accepted students this bracket is common but still less frequent than upper-middle income. Finally, your LSAT score of 34 fell short of the 37.18 average seen in successful applicants, adding a further push toward a failing outcome.

Taken together, these academic and background signals led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. 

To improve your chances, focus first on raising your academic record. Retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-37 range and strengthening your overall GPA through additional coursework would directly address the two most influential factors. Consider also whether part-time study options or targeted bar-prep resources could help offset the risk the model identified.
